The data

These pages use version 3.1.0 of the Russian Financial Statements Database (RFSD), an open collection of annual unconsolidated financial statements linked to the Russian legal-entity register. The adopted files hold 63,308,662 annual records for 2011 to 2025. Rosstat supplied the statements for 2012 to 2018 and the Federal Tax Service (FNS) those from 2019. The pages therefore treat the Rosstat years and the FNS years as separate periods, and no year-to-year comparison crosses 2019.

Financial year dates the accounts. The archive records their availability in one release. Under the 2022 procedure a firm could request closure of public access to all its statements from 2019 onward. From 2023, firms could also request restrictions for specific reporting years. Both financial years in a comparison come from the same release. A restriction that removed statements for earlier years as well as later ones therefore cannot be counted from their difference. The archive does not record when public access changed.

In the dissertation: Section 1.4.1, Section 2.2.1, Section 1.4.4

* The archive holds no filed statements for 2011. Statements for 2025, the latest year, are filed on revised official forms, and 2025 is reported as an extension of 2019 to 2024. In the dissertation: Section 1.4.4, Section 2.2.1

Terms

Statement available
A filed statement counts as available unless the RFSD identifies it as imputed from a later filing. Files without that designation are treated as non-imputed. A statement can be absent because it was never filed, contained only zeros, was imputed, or was closed to public access. A filed statement flagged for anomalous amounts still counts as available. Its amounts are excluded from financial measures and asset ranks.
All eligible firms
Every firm the provider marks as eligible in the financial year, with or without a statement. The provider's classification can differ from a firm's legal duty to file.
Registered at year-end
The eligible firms still registered at the end of the year. Neither population is a panel of the same firms, because firms enter, leave, and change eligibility.
Transition
One year in the history of a firm eligible and registered at the preceding year-end. The figure shows firms still eligible and registered with or without a statement, and firms removed from the register. The shares use all transitions, including cases in which eligibility ended or the firm's status could not be resolved.
Ownership
Private firms, firms with foreign or joint ownership, state-related firms, and others, as the registry records each firm in each year. State-related ownership groups the registry's codes for state or municipal ownership, mixed ownership with state participation, and state-corporation ownership, and the codes do not establish operational control.
State and municipal enterprises
Firms registered under the legal form called unitary enterprise, which operate publicly owned assets and issue no shares.
The five lists
The sanctions list, the Russian government's list of strategic firms, the Russian president's list of strategic firms, the 2020 filing-exemption list, and the decree list. Each is matched to the RFSD by taxpayer identifier, and membership is held fixed across years because the lists carry no verified dates. Firms on no list are those matched to none of the five.
Asset quintiles
Firms eligible and registered at both year-ends with positive assets on an unflagged statement for the preceding year. Ranking them by those assets gives five groups of roughly equal size, called quintiles. Q1 contains the smallest firms and Q5 the largest. The annual comparison forms the groups anew each year. The comparison following firms through 2024 keeps their 2021 groups.
The cash sample and the inventory sample
Eligible nonfinancial firms whose unflagged 2021 statement reports positive sales and assets, with cash (1,503,173 firms) or with inventories (1,179,317 firms), and with measured age and a consistent identifier. The samples follow these firms through 2024 without conditions on later reporting or registration. Each estimate uses the members with the outcomes it requires.
Symmetric revenue growth
The change in real sales divided by average sales at the two dates, expressed in points. It admits a recorded fall to zero. Missing sales remain unobserved.

In the dissertation: Section 2.2.1, Section 2.2.2, Section 2.2.3, Section 1.4.5, Section 3.2

Models

Chapter 2 uses separate logit models for statement availability in the Rosstat and FNS years. The models account for financial year and hold constant the firm's age, two-digit industry, region, legal form, and ownership. An odds ratio compares two groups at the same values of the other regressors. Above one, the first group is more likely to have a statement, and below one, less likely.

The list comparisons also report average predicted probabilities. These averages use observations from the estimation sample whose industries, regions, legal forms, ownership categories, and ages are represented in both groups. For each of those observations, the model predicts availability once under membership in the list in question alone and once under membership in none of the five lists. The difference between the two averages gives the gap in predicted availability.

Chapter 3 compares firms by their cash and inventory shares, by ownership, and by the foreign share of their industry. Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML) fits expected real revenue in levels, so firms with larger sales can have more influence. Its estimates are percentage differences in the ratio of expected end-year to expected reference-year revenue. Ordinary least squares gives each firm equal weight in comparisons of symmetric revenue growth and changes in operating margin. The margin estimates are in percentage points.

The replacement regression compares four-digit industries within the same two-digit industry, with opening industry sales as weights. Its slope measures how much more other firms' sales changed where firms with foreign or joint ownership lost an additional ruble. A slope of one corresponds to full replacement at the margin. The association does not identify which customers changed suppliers.

The dissertation also uses inverse probability weights to examine missing outcomes. An observed firm receives more weight when its 2021 characteristics predict a lower probability of observing its later outcome. This requires outcomes to be missing at random given those characteristics, a correctly specified observation model, and positive observation probabilities.

Intervals on every page are individual 95% confidence intervals. Chapter 2 uses standard errors clustered by two-digit industry and region. Its predicted probabilities and probability gaps are descriptive summaries. Chapter 3 uses the same clustering for resource and ownership comparisons, four-digit industry clusters for private incumbents, and two-digit industry clusters for replacement regressions. The estimates are conditional associations, and the dissertation's design sections state what each comparison can identify.
